item.title: Rapid weight loss on popular drugs could ‘starve’ the brain, expert warns
item.description: Dr. Tommy Wood warns GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy can shrink brain tissue when caloric restriction cuts off vital energy the brain needs.
item.content:encoded:
As GLP-1 weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy continue to surge in popularity, experts warn that rapid weight loss and severe caloric restriction could deprive the brain of vital energy and nutrients.

Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, said the drugs' effects on the brain may depend on whether the body is getting enough energy and nutrients during weight loss.

"The best way to think about this is the spectrum of what we call energy availability," Wood told Fox News Digital at Strong NY, New York City's largest annual fitness and wellness festival. "The brain is your most energy-hungry organ in the body."

POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER

According to Wood, brain reserve — the physical amount and integrity of brain tissue — follows a bell-shaped curve relative to the body's energy availability.

Excess energy caused by obesity, high blood sugar and metabolic disease can lower the brain's resilience by damaging blood vessels and contributing to insulin resistance.

In these cases, GLP-1 medications can provide cognitive benefits by lowering blood pressure and improving blood sugar control.

However, Wood noted that the lower end of the energy spectrum poses its own structural risks to the brain. Because the brain relies heavily on continuous fuel, extreme caloric deficits can force the organ to consume its own tissue.

POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS CAN BECOME AN ‘ATOMIC BOMB’ AT HIGH DOSES, DOCTOR WARNS

"There was a study that looked at the brains of people who ran a marathon ... because the marathon is so energy-intensive, the white matter in the brain actually shrank during a marathon because the brain didn't have enough energy … so it was eating its own white matter," Wood said, noting that the participants' brains recovered after resting and refueling.

"It just shows that the brain is really energy-hungry, and it will decrease its size if it's not getting enough energy."

Concerns about lean muscle loss when taking GLP-1 medications are often nuanced, Wood said. Some of the early "lean mass" that's lost is actually fat that had built up inside the muscles.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"So technically, your muscles get smaller, but you don't get weaker," he told Fox News Digital. "And the quality and functioning of your muscles actually gets better."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

However, risks arise when individuals taking GLP-1 medications drastically reduce their food intake for extended periods. Chronic under-eating can deprive the central nervous system of essential structural nutrients, Wood warned.

"It is possible that you can end up going too far," he said. "If you're not eating enough, you're not getting the nutrients that are critical for the brain. So you're not getting in enough omega-3 fats, which we know are really important. You're not getting enough iron and protein and all those kinds of things."

To safeguard brain health while losing weight, Wood recommends pairing weight-loss regimens with resistance training twice a week to maintain functional muscle mass and to stimulate brain growth factors.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Additionally, ensuring adequate intake of core "neuro-nutrients" — including B vitamins (B12, folate, B6), vitamin D, iron and omega-3 fatty acids — prevents long-term cognitive impairment, according to Wood.

"For most people, I think it's going to be beneficial to start, but you just need to make sure that you don't push it too far, that you're now getting enough of everything that the brain needs," he advised.

item.title: US Department of Education data reveals 1,100 sexual assault allegations against public school staff
item.description: Roughly 1,100 allegations of rape or sexual assault were made against public school employees in 2023-24, with 320 staff members resigning first.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Department of Education released new data showing that approximately 1,100 allegations of rape, attempted rape or sexual assault were made against public school employees during the 2023-24 school year. The revelations come amid the department's ongoing efforts to protect women and children, with a focus on enforcing Title IX across the country.

The figures were included in the department’s latest Civil Rights Data Collection, a mandatory survey covering more than 17,000 public school districts and 97,000 schools nationwide.

Of the roughly 1,100 allegations against staff members, approximately 320 resulted in an employee resigning or retiring before any final disciplinary action or termination, according to the report. About 280 resulted in findings that the employee was not responsible, 230 remained pending and 200 resulted in findings of responsibility. Approximately 90 led to duty reassignment before final disciplinary action or termination.

FORMER NEW JERSEY MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHER INDICTED ON NEW CHARGES INCLUDING MANUFACTURING CHILD ABUSE MATERIAL

"Parents deserve to know that when they send their children to school, their safety comes first," Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kim Richey said in a statement.

"The Civil Rights Data Collection gives us critical information to identify potential failures to protect students and hold school districts accountable when concerns arise," Richey continued. "Thanks to President Trump and Secretary McMahon’s leadership, the Office for Civil Rights will continue to follow the facts, enforce federal civil rights laws, and ensure schools take their responsibility to protect students seriously."

School districts separately reported approximately 11,800 incidents of rape, attempted rape or other sexual assault during the 2023-24 school year. About 460, or roughly 4%, were reported as having been committed by school staff.

EDUCATION DEPARTMENT RESCINDS BIDEN TITLE IX RULE, RESTORES TRUMP-ERA REGULATIONS

The department cautioned that the number of reported incidents and the number of allegations against staff are separate measurements. It also said reporting in this area is still developing. The staff sexual-offense questions were first included as optional elements in the 2020-21 collection and became mandatory for 2023-24.

The findings come after the department’s Office for Civil Rights launched a national K-12 initiative in July aimed at protecting students from sexual misconduct by adults in schools. The initiative included 20 directed investigations of districts that the department said appeared to have inadequately addressed staff-on-student sexual misconduct. ed.gov

The department said schools that fail to respond appropriately to sexual harassment or abuse may violate Title IX and could face enforcement action, including the potential loss of federal funding.

Trump's Department of Education, under McMahon's leadership, has made the protection of women and children a focus.

The department announced at the beginning of Trump’s second term that it would enforce the 2020 Title IX regulations after a federal court vacated the Biden administration’s 2024 rewrite. On Monday, the department formally removed the vacated Biden-era rule from the Code of Federal Regulations and restored the earlier regulatory language. The 2020 regulations establish requirements for how federally funded schools must respond to allegations of sexual harassment and assault while providing due-process protections for accused students.

The administration has also directed federal agencies to interpret sex-based protections according to biological sex rather than gender identity. Trump’s January 2025 executive order defines "woman" as an adult human female and "girl" as a juvenile human female, while defining sex as an immutable biological classification. The Education Department subsequently instructed its Office for Civil Rights to enforce Title IX consistent with those definitions.

That approach has guided the department’s enforcement efforts involving women’s sports, sex-separated facilities and schools’ responses to sexual misconduct. Title IX prohibits sex discrimination in education programs and activities receiving federal funding, and institutions found in violation can ultimately risk losing that assistance if they refuse to comply.

The administration has also made preserving women’s sports a central part of its Title IX agenda. Trump signed an executive order in February 2025 directing federal agencies to oppose male participation in women’s athletic competition, while the Education Department has opened investigations and pursued enforcement actions against schools and athletic organizations whose policies it says deny female athletes equal opportunities, privacy or safety.

item.title: Former Israeli PM hails ‘heroism’ after passengers help thwart alleged cockpit attack
item.description: Naftali Bennett says Israeli passengers jumped into the cockpit to stop the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the pilot on a Dubai flight to Tel Aviv.
item.content:encoded:
Former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett credited the quick-thinking actions of passengers and crew for thwarting what officials are investigating as a possible terrorist attack Wednesday after an alleged cockpit stabbing sent an Israel-bound passenger plane into a nosedive.

"This wasn't a miracle. It was an act of heroism by the passengers and of the Emirati crew," Bennett told "The Faulkner Focus."

"It's people who saved the day, people who showed courage, who didn't stand passively but took action, and I'm so darn proud to be Israeli today."

UNITED FLIGHT FROM CHICAGO MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER PASSENGER'S 'MULTIPLE ATTEMPTS' TO BREACH COCKPIT

The original flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where the passengers were transferred to another plane. Those who were aboard during the incident later arrived at Ben Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv.

Bennett thanked Saudi authorities for allowing the aircraft to make an emergency landing and caring for those on board while they were on the ground.

Though details are still emerging, Bennett cited Israeli authorities in detailing that the flight was traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when the co-pilot allegedly attacked the pilot with a pocketknife and tried to bring down the aircraft, sending it into a steep descent.

That's when, Bennett said, Israeli passengers sprang into action.

RETIRED POLICE CHIEF HELPS SUBDUE PASSENGER AFTER ALLEGED MIDAIR OUTBURST OVER ALCOHOL CUTOFF

"A couple of passengers, Israeli citizens, jumped into the cockpit," he said. "They took over the alleged terrorist, pulled him out, and they sent in the second crew that was [on] standby."

The attacked pilot can be seen bleeding and wearing an oxygen mask while lying on his back in graphic footage from the incident. Saudi Arabia's Tabuk Airport said both pilots were hospitalized with injuries, according to Reuters.

Israeli officials are investigating whether the incident was an attempted terrorist attack.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the incident Wednesday, praising those who jumped into action.

"I salute the heroes who showed extraordinary bravery and, according to the passenger's account, saved many lives," Netanyahu said, according to an unofficial translation of his remarks.

He added that the pilot accused of carrying out the stabbing had been arrested and was being questioned by Saudi authorities.

Fox News' Bradford Betz contributed to this report.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: Peggy Flanagan's DEI record and fraud scandal put Minnesota Senate race in the spotlight

"The lieutenant governor [Peggy Flanagan], even as we sit here today, continues to take absolutely no accountability for any of the fraud issues, and she continues to blame the governor. And I'm going to be honest: It's p---ing me off."

The above quote is not from a Republican, but from Democratic Rep. Angie Craig in July when she was running in the Minnesota Senate primary against Peggy Flanagan. While harsh words are often lightly thrown in primary battles, in this case, one must ask: Where is the lie?

While Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Colorado’s House candidate Milot Kiros have snagged headlines for their far-left views, Flanagan has been able to hide a bit.

However, the tightening race in Minnesota, as shown both through on-the-ground reporting and in polling, is putting Democrats everywhere in an awkward position because they had thought Flanagan’s leftist lunacy would float under the radar this cycle.

Well, not anymore.

DAVID MARCUS: IN DEEP BLUE MINNESOTA A RED DAWN MAY BE RISING AHEAD OF THE MIDTERMS

Now that the Gopher State is firmly in the political spotlight, voters will be reminded, for example, of Flanagan wearing a T-shirt that says "Protect Trans Kids" on it, with a picture of a large Bowie knife — which can only be rationally read as a threat of physical violence.

We know what the shirt means because not just threats, but also acts of physical violence by, or in defense of, members of the trans community have become commonplace in our society. Harry Potter author J.K. Rowling is threatened constantly for simply believing that men cannot become women.

PEGGY FLANAGAN VOWS TO 'RIP ICE APART' AFTER TOPPLING MODERATE DEM IN KEY SENATE BATTLE

Among the farcical programs created by this unhinged rubric was Minnesota’s marijuana legalization efforts that gave loans, often forgivable, to people based on "special equity status," to open dispensaries — many of which have now failed and closed.

Truly, only government leftists could foul up selling weed, something mastered by the stoners we all knew in high school.

Of course, this emphasis on "special equity" and DEI also lies at the root of Flanagan’s massive Somali fraud scandal, where whistleblowers were ignored as hundreds of millions, at least, were pilfered because Peggy was uncomfortable criticizing Somalis.

To make matters worse, some of the alleged fraudsters appear to be inside Flanagan’s inner circle, including Nimco Ahmed, with whom Flanagan recently appeared in full hijab, no less, whose autism center is now under investigation.

Tafoya has taken her middle-of-the-road message on a media blitz in recent weeks. One half expects her to be interviewed on Prairie Home Companion, while Flanagan has all but been in hiding, entertaining only the most comfortable and coddling interviews possible.

Notwithstanding the fact that early voting has already begun in Minnesota, a month is too long for Flanagan to pull a Biden-esque hide-in-the-basement strategy, especially as Tafoya’s national profile is only growing stronger.

To date, Flanagan has not agreed to debate the eager Tafoya, presumably for all the reasons, reflecting her failed record. But at this point, refusing to take on her opponent face-to-face might play worse than any embarrassment the event itself might cause.

The Democrats have a Peggy Flanagan problem. They really, really, really don’t want her and her bizarre brand of progressivism on the Sunday shows, but at this point, they may have no choice.

Meanwhile, for Michele Tafoya and Minnesotans, what once looked like a long shot is now very close to even money.

item.title: Aaron Sorkin reveals why Trump is unmentioned in 'Social Reckoning' movie
item.description: Director Aaron Sorkin revealed why President Donald Trump's name was deliberately cut from "The Social Reckoning," his new film exploring Facebook's role in polarization.
item.content:encoded:
Writer-director Aaron Sorkin explained why President Donald Trump’s name is omitted from his upcoming film examining Facebook’s influence on political discourse, including in the lead-up to the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot.

When asked by Politico why Trump is not mentioned, Sorkin said he believed the president’s inclusion would become an unwelcome "distraction," adding that it was his decision to keep his name out of the film and that he wanted "clean hands."

"I felt like as soon as we got to that scene, as soon as you saw anything ‘Trump,’ it would just become about something else," Sorkin told the outlet. "Again, I realize it’s going to kind of become about that ‘something else’ anyway. But I just like to have clean hands."

'THE SOCIAL RECKONING' TRAILER DROPS WITH JEREMY STRONG AS ZUCKERBERG IN AARON SORKIN'S FACEBOOK SEQUEL

"The Social Reckoning," set to premiere in theaters Oct. 9, 2026, is a companion piece to Sorkin’s 2010 film "The Social Network," which chronicled the rise of Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg.

The new movie follows whistleblower Frances Haugen, who provided internal Facebook documents to The Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, which became the basis for the outlet's "Facebook Files" series examining the company's internal research and practices. 

The documents, published as part of a 2021 investigative series for the Journal, included internal research and findings about political polarization and the effects of Instagram on some young users' mental health.

Sorkin acknowledged that the film is "political" but argued that it is "not a red-blue thing."

BIPARTISAN LAWMAKERS WANT TO STRIP BIG TECH'S LEGAL IMMUNITY THAT CAN SHIELD SOCIAL MEDIA COMPANIES

He said he wasn't directed to remove Trump's name from the movie but instead kept him out of it to keep Facebook at the center of the discussion.

"I’m not going to deny, of course, that the movie is political. I just think it shouldn’t be. There’s really no reason for it to be," the screenwriter said.

"I delivered the script and I think the next day I was in Tom Rothman’s office, and unsolicited, I told him that in that sequence we wouldn’t see any Trump signage at all. We won’t even see red hats. We’re going to see "Don’t Tread on Me," "Stop the Steal." You see American flags, Confederate flags, but it won’t be about MAGA versus everybody else, or even red-blue. It’s just going to be about Facebook’s role in the rise of divisiveness, extremism, and hyperpartisanship. So it was my choice. "

A spokesperson for Meta said in 2022 that the platform was not responsible for violence on Jan. 6, instead pointing to Trump and others who promoted false claims that the 2020 election had been stolen.

EX-NYPD INSPECTOR WARNS SOCIAL MEDIA LIKELY HELPED POLITICAL VIOLENCE ‘METASTASIZE’ INTO WHCD SCARE

The film arrives as technology companies face continued scrutiny over social media’s harmful effects and as artificial intelligence draws attention in Washington.

Social media’s influence has grown considerably in the 16 years since "The Social Network" was released and "The Social Reckoning" returns to Facebook to examine allegations about the platform’s role in amplifying political division and extremist content.

Sorkin said he had considered revisiting Facebook whenever the company was in the news, but the story involving Haugen and Horwitz finally felt like a solid basis for a film.

"The fact that the film has coincided with what tech people would call an inflection point is just happenstance," he said as his movie arrives to a more tech-skeptical audience in 2026.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

"The Social Reckoning" is set to be released Oct. 9, roughly one month before the 2026 midterm elections. Sorkin told Politico that the upcoming elections played a part in deciding when the film would be released.

"I don’t think this movie can change the course of electoral history," the filmmaker explained. "But these midterms are why I didn’t want to wait a year to make the movie. I didn’t want the movie to come out after the midterms because I didn’t think we’d be in the mood for it anymore."

"And yeah, I thought maybe one little reminder might be helpful," he added.

An insider close to the White House panned the movie as "delusional fiction."

"Trump-deranged Democrats like Sorkin live in a political bubble that pathetically now encapsulates their art," they told Fox News Digital. "Judging by the trailers released, this delusional fiction looks so bad, it may even have the opposite effect of what was intended. What a loser!"

Fox News Digital reached out to Meta and the White House for comment.

item.title: FBI hack claim raises fears over sensitive personal data
item.description: ShinyHunters claims it breached FBIJobs.gov and stole Social Security numbers, home addresses and sensitive assignment details of FBI personnel.
item.content:encoded:
If you have ever filled out a job application, handed over your Social Security number for a background check or trusted an organization with information about your family, pay attention to what happened at the FBI.

The cybercriminal group ShinyHunters claims it compromised FBIJobs.gov and stole highly sensitive information connected to current and former FBI personnel and people who applied for jobs at the bureau. The group says its haul reaches far beyond basic contact information.

On Sept. 23, the FBI acknowledged the group's claims and said it was "actively and aggressively investigating" the incident. The bureau said investigators had not yet determined whether the point of breach involved an FBI system or a third-party provider supporting FBIJobs.gov. 

That uncertainty is important. At the same time, samples provided to journalists contain enough real-world information to make the situation difficult to dismiss. For anyone whose details may be included, the potential fallout goes well beyond having an email address leaked.

FBI SAYS SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED

Since that statement, the FBI has struck back by announcing the arrest of an alleged ShinyHunters leader in the Netherlands after a joint operation with Dutch authorities. Dutch police said a 24-year-old Amsterdam man was arrested Sept. 15.

In its Sept. 23 statement, the FBI addressed both the alleged compromise and the uncertainty surrounding where the attackers may have gained access. 

"The FBI is aware of a cybercriminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the fbijobs.gov portal," the bureau said. It added that the point of breach remained undetermined and said it was "actively and aggressively investigating this matter." 

The FBI also said investigators were working closely with third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to reduce potential risk. The FBI confirmed the investigation and the unresolved question about where the breach occurred. It did not verify ShinyHunters' full account of what the group says it stole.

The FBI's Special Agent Applicant Portal also became unavailable as the incident unfolded. A notice posted Sept. 22 said FBIJobs.gov and the Special Agent Applicant Portal were unavailable. The applicant portal supports people who have progressed through portions of the special-agent hiring process, making the type of information potentially involved especially sensitive.

CyberGuy reached out to the FBI for an update on the incident, including whether employee or applicant data was accessed and whether affected individuals are being notified or offered identity protection. We did not hear back before our deadline.

ShinyHunters provided journalists with a spreadsheet containing about 5,000 alleged FBI personnel records. Reuters reported that the spreadsheet included names, home addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, Social Security numbers and emergency contact information. It also included information about field office assignments and, in some cases, sensitive intelligence or counterespionage work.

Reuters said it could not authenticate the entire spreadsheet. However, reporters independently verified details belonging to more than 22 people by comparing the information with credit records and earlier leaked data. Reuters also matched career information or job titles for eight people against court filings, news reports, public profiles and online posts.

That still does not establish where every record came from. Real information can appear in several databases or previous breaches. Yet the matches add credibility to at least portions of the sample. 404 Media separately reported that the 5,000-person sample contained names, home addresses, phone numbers and information involving FBI employees' spouses.

The personal information alone creates obvious privacy concerns. The reported job information raises another level of risk. Reuters found records identifying people connected to China-related investigations, Russian intelligence work, human intelligence operations and electronic surveillance. Other entries referenced covert access, clandestine technical operations and telecommunications interception. Reuters said it could not verify that every assignment was authentic or up to date.

On Sept. 23, 404 Media also reported that the data appeared to expose members of the FBI's Remote Operations Unit. The outlet describes the ROU as a secretive FBI team involved in developing and using hacking tools to gain access to target devices. Think about what that combination of information could provide to someone with bad intentions. 

A name may lead to a home address. An emergency contact could identify a spouse or child. Job information might reveal the kind of investigations someone works on. For an FBI employee working in a sensitive position, that creates risks far beyond ordinary financial fraud.

IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB?

ShinyHunters says it breached the FBI and stole between 2 and 3 terabytes of information connected to FBI personnel and job applicants. The group has also claimed that Justice Department worker data was obtained. The hackers claim they exploited a previously unknown vulnerability involving Oracle PeopleSoft, software used for human resources and other enterprise functions.

FBI documents reportedly show its recruiting operation uses PeopleSoft and AWS GovCloud. However, that does not prove the hackers' claimed method of attack. The alleged PeopleSoft vulnerability, the claimed 2-to-3-terabyte haul and a broader compromise of FBI systems had not been independently verified.

Reuters also reported that ShinyHunters claimed to possess files involving employee and applicant vetting, contracted background investigations and sensitive medical information. Reuters said it could not verify what additional information the hackers actually possessed. That caveat is critical. ShinyHunters has an obvious interest in making its access sound as extensive as possible. For now, there are signs that portions of the information supplied by the hackers correspond to real people. Major questions about the source, scope and attack path remain unresolved in the FBI's public statement.

ShinyHunters says retaliation, rather than a demand for money, motivated the attack. The group points to warnings the FBI issued about ShinyHunters-related cyber activity earlier in 2026. On May 15, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center published an advisory describing ShinyHunters as a cybercriminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion.

The advisory warned that actors using the name may use real or exaggerated claims about stolen information to pressure victims. It also described threatening communications, harassment of family members and swatting among tactics associated with ShinyHunters actors. ShinyHunters disputes portions of the FBI's description of its activities. Reuters reported that the group said it targeted the FBI because of the May warning and said it was holding the allegedly stolen data while demanding that the bureau rescind the statement.

You may read a headline about FBI employees and assume this has little to do with you. Yet the way the alleged data could be abused should feel familiar to anyone who has handed personal information to an employer, bank, health provider, insurance company or government agency. Organizations often collect far more than your name and email address. They may hold your home address, Social Security number, birthdate, employment history and emergency contacts. Job applications can contain years of background information.

You may have done everything right and still have that information exposed because the organization holding it or one of its technology providers was attacked. That third-party piece deserves attention here. In its Sept. 23 statement, the FBI specifically said investigators had not determined whether the breach point involved its own enterprise or a third party.

The same setup exists throughout everyday life. Your employer might use an outside payroll provider. Your doctor's office may rely on billing software from another company. Retailers routinely send information through outside payment systems. Once you hand over your personal data, you often have little visibility into how many systems eventually store or process it.

Suppose someone emails you and knows your full name, employer and home address. Then the person mentions your spouse or a job application you actually submitted. That message feels very different from a generic scam email. This is why personal data can be so useful to attackers. They can combine stolen records with information already available from data brokers, social media or previous breaches. The result can be a phishing message tailored closely enough to make you hesitate before questioning it.

Cybercriminals could pose as an FBI recruiter or someone from an employer's human resources department. They could even claim they are contacting you to help protect information exposed in the breach. The FBI's May advisory warned that stolen personal information can help attackers create targeted campaigns and pressure victims.

Even while investigators work to establish the full scope, anyone who believes their information may be involved can take precautions.

If you applied for an FBI job, be suspicious of calls, texts or emails claiming you need to reenter information because of the portal incident. Do not use a link or phone number contained in an unexpected message. Contact your existing applicant coordinator or reach the FBI through a channel you already know. The FBI's own ShinyHunters guidance recommends verifying unusual requests through another method before responding.

This step becomes particularly important because the reported sample included spouses and emergency contacts. Tell people listed on employment or application records to be cautious if someone suddenly knows their connection to you. Criminals may target a relative because they expect that person to have fewer security safeguards. If someone claims there is an urgent problem involving you, an employer or law enforcement, verify the story independently before sharing information or sending money.

A credit freeze can make it harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name. You need to place the freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. The FTC says credit freezes are free and remain in place until you lift them. A freeze will not prevent every form of identity theft. Continue monitoring accounts you already have.

If your Social Security number may have been exposed, an IRS Identity Protection PIN can help protect you from tax identity theft. The six-digit IP PIN prevents someone else from filing a federal tax return using your Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number. Anyone with an SSN or ITIN who can verify their identity can request one. Keep the number private. The IRS says it will never call, email or text you asking for your IP PIN.

Look for new accounts you do not recognize, unfamiliar charges or changes to existing accounts. Also pay attention to unexpected IRS notices, rejected tax filings and medical bills or insurance explanations of benefits for treatment you never received. These can signal types of identity theft that a credit freeze alone may not stop. If you discover identity theft, report it through IdentityTheft.gov and follow the recovery plan for the information that was compromised.

Neither Reuters nor the FBI's Sept. 23 statement said passwords were included in the 5,000-record sample. Still, exposed personal details can make attempts to steal your passwords much more convincing. Use a unique password for every important account. A password manager can help keep track of them. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) or passkeys wherever available. Also be cautious about unexpected password-reset requests.

A personalized phishing message can still contain a malicious link or infected attachment. Strong antivirus software can help detect known phishing websites, malicious downloads and malware before they compromise your device. That gives you another layer of protection if a convincing email or text gets through. Security software cannot replace careful clicking, but it can help when a scam looks unusually believable. If your home address, phone number and relatives already appear on people search sites, leaked records can give criminals even more information to work with. Search for yourself online and review what is publicly visible. You can request removal from many data broker and people search sites yourself or use a personal data removal service to handle recurring opt-out requests. Reducing what is publicly available gives a criminal fewer pieces to combine with information from a breach. Dark web monitoring can alert you when information tied to your email address, phone number, Social Security number or other identifiers appears in known breach collections. Some identity theft companies include Dark Web Monitoring that searches for exposed personal information and alerts you when it is found. However, treat an alert as a warning rather than proof that someone has stolen your identity. Monitoring cannot prevent information from circulating once criminals obtain it. Its value comes from giving you an opportunity to secure affected accounts, watch for fraud and take action sooner. See my tips and best picks on best identity theft protection at CyberGuy.com.

The FBI's guidance involving ShinyHunters recommends against paying or engaging with threat actors making demands. Save threatening communications instead. Preserve screenshots, email addresses, phone numbers and other identifying information. You can report cybercrime through the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov. If someone appears to face an immediate physical threat, contact emergency services.

There are still major unanswered questions about the FBIJobs.gov incident. The FBI's Sept. 23 statement left the point of breach unresolved, and the bureau had not publicly validated ShinyHunters' claim that it stole between 2 and 3 terabytes of data. Still, the data samples deserve serious attention. Reuters verified details belonging to more than 22 people and reported that the spreadsheet contained Social Security numbers, home addresses, dates of birth, emergency contacts and information about sensitive assignments. What concerns me most is how useful those pieces become when they are connected. 

A criminal who knows where you work, where you live and who your spouse is has a much easier time building a scam that feels authentic. For FBI personnel tied to intelligence or covert technical work, the exposure could create security concerns that reach well beyond financial fraud. The takeaway for the rest of us is practical. You cannot control the security of every employer, government agency or company holding your information. You can control how much information about you remains publicly available, how strongly your accounts are protected and how quickly you respond when something suspicious appears.
